Tomb of the Bloodletter brings an external skill base into roguelike deck builders, something I personally haven't seen before. Unfortunately for me that skill is scrabble, which I am awful at. In spite of my 4th grade spelling capacity I am currently enjoying this game with few complaints so far. The game both mitigates the frustration and embraces the excitement of RNG in its progression scheme, and in doing so the game feels fresh on each run. The art style is simple yet cohesive, and information is succinctly conveyed through the UI. My only major complaint so far is that the time between choosing your loot and starting the next fight is a tad lengthy, but that's more of an aesthetic frustration than a gameplay one. While I received the game for free, this game seems to be a good deal for the price, especially if you like vocabulary games. Just keep a tab open to google spell check.
I can't spell, I don't know why I bought this.

This is a game I'm having a very hard time going between liking and not, and whether to recommend or not for that matter. I do think the enjoyment I had with this game is enough for me to give it a positive recommendation, albeit with the caveat that it is a VERY difficult game. The game is very fun once you're immersed in the challenge the game gives. It encourages really trying out different vocabulary in different fights and honestly has been really great at learning better typing skills due to the amount of different words can be used against a different run, it has a very charming art style to boot and enemies on their own can provide a very nice breath of fresh air that prevent from spamming the same word every time and just winning. The game has a really interesting depth to it's easy to recommend it on those front's, especially considering the low price tag. Yet, despite of that recommendation, The game does have some flaws. My biggest problem to date is probably the severity to which healing is limited to, every tick of damage is almost permanent as you don't recover any between enemy encounters unless you take the "caveat healing" Magiks (what the game's special effect tiles are called); if you even healed a little health between encounters it would genuinely go a long way towards this game going from "brutally difficult" to "Fun level of difficulty." On top of the healing though, you're unable to see what enemy is coming up next which makes map traversal extremely punishing, you can choose tiles that go towards your build, get countered on one encounter, and be forced to keep the chosen path, compounding with limited healing, it just makes luck matter so much more than any skill or knowledge you might have. My last major complaint is just that unless you choose the map tile that gives you a free Magik, every Magik you receive from defeating an enemy comes with a heavy modification to the next fight, from taking damage (which is again difficult to recover), Lowering your max health (Makes any healing even harder), or even disabling a significant chunk of letters from being used, which CAN be a fun challenge, but it only adds to the already high difficulty of the encounters you have to face. I still find I do give this game a recommendation, a cautious one at that but a recommendation nonetheless, and I'm really excited to see how the developer takes the game from here!

Once you've seen past a lot of the immediate challenge of Tomb of the Bloodletter, and you understand the roguelike structure of it, you finally encounter the game's toughest challenge: trying to spell chipolte

I feel like this game could get a recommend but there are a few things that limit it. The premise is like many rogue-likes you run through over and over, getting upgrades and tools to make it easier as you go along. But, this game doesn't do that. Your upgrades ALWAYS come with a downside. You must take damage or let your opponent get stronger to get mediocre spells. The spells are distributed randomly, meaning if they land right you can unleash a massive combo... Once. Then you hope they land on letters that let you make a coherent word that does something. But if it lands in such a way that you can't make good use of each letter? You can waste moves entirely. You get 2 reshuffles on your first guy and the second lets you pay life to reshuffle. Great, but then you end up with 3 missteps, which cause you 1 damage each time they're used, and they don't go away until used. That is another wasted turn. You can use the Peace spell to reduce damage. But you can't go to 0 damage. Why? I don't get to generate armor or guarantee healing or my own damage. Why do I get penalized for bad RNG? Finally, I feel like the letters should get inherent bonuses themselves. Z, Q, X, etc like scrabble, should get a bonus. Something, double power one time on each letter. Or make distribution favor them less.

I truly wish I could recommend this game. But for me the thing that makes a rogue lite game bearable through all the failures is that it feels like it's at least my fault and that my personal skill improving will improve the quality of my runs. That does not seem to be the case here. Be it a failure of, or a lack of, game logic, you're repeatedly dealt unwinnable hands and it just doesn't feel good; it doesn't help that you gain nothing from the failure but a sense that you should play another game for a sense of accomplishment.

small edit: a theme with a lot of the negative reviews is that they didn't understand the Fury mechanic. where you can damage yourself to gain an increase to all damage you deal during a given fight; in other words, *self-damage is a deliberate and well-thought-out mechanic, abilities don't cause self-damage just because the game hates you, and engaging with it is often necessary to do well in the game*. this is why many abilities involve damaging yourself to some degree, these reviews likely indicate that Fury could've been explained better in the game, and i could definitely see that argument; but it is entirely a reasonable game mechanic. just wanted to preface this review by addressing this specific point ——— easily my favorite word-based roguelike i've tried so far. it differentiates itself (from the ones i've tried and subsequently lost interest in) by not trying to be scrabble-flavored balatro, but something altogether different. the game does not, by default, limit the letters you can use. you can write any up-to-12-letter word you can think of, but you must account for the magicks—what keys are they on right now? what order do you want them to activate in? how many times can you use this letter in a single word, so that the magick procs multiple times for this usage? should you leave a magick on a certain key so that you can use it in a later turn instead? considerations like these make the game feel quite dynamic in a way that others haven't, to me. of course, on top of this, Bloodletter is oriented around a combat system in which you must manage your health and healing, fury (a meter which adds +1 damage to your attacks whenever you damage yourself for 4 health), and things which attack or debuff the enemy. different magicks play with these mechanics in different ways, and finding the right word to do exactly the combination of magicks you need is massively satisfying. the fact that word length or complexity isn't a constant factor feels good; play the word that does what you need it to. sometimes that will be a long and obscure word that tests your vocabulary, and other times, it'll be a simple one with 4 letters or less. the magicks get distributed randomly onto the keyboard, and, while this can sometimes lead to "bad hands," you can use a resource called "prayers" to get a new "hand", helping to mitigate the effect of sheer randomness. i think it needs to be there to some degree to prevent overly static strategies from trivializing the game. there are also tools you can acquire from carpenter rooms, which are items you can activate when you need them, separate from the magicks on your keyboard. additionally, there are various status effects in the game, such as one that prevents you from using an afflicted letter; these statuses (often inflicted by enemies) are generally the only thing that will limit your letter selection, which is fair. indeed, the way enemies are designed in this game, i often feel like i have to approach each one noticeably differently than the others (especially on later floors). all of these factors serve to add a good deal of variety to the your runs. you are also tasked to create a word at the start of each of the 3 floors which will define the rewards you get after each fight (with at least a couple room types guaranteed to be vowels, so as to prevent empty rooms being unavoidable). i have so far always been able to create a word that has a reward after each room, though it's usually difficult to get exactly what i want, which is, again, fair. every room will also permit you to choose a new magick regardless of the kind of room you were in, though these are always accompanied with some extra effect (usually a bad effect if the magick is good, and maybe a more positive effect for a more mediocre one). some negative reviews have said that this feels like you're always punished for trying to improve your deck, but this is not the case with the room-based rewards (including the room that gives you a choice between 5 magicks), not to mention most of the negative effects only last for 1 fight, so i don't think that makes sense to say. you are also allowed to opt not to take a magick in this way a limited number of times. the presentation is really charming, i think. i quite enjoy the art and sound design/OST, and the enemy designs are fun. i will say, one thing that's a little disappointing is that, as things are right now, the runs seem to just kind of End—but i also have not beaten a basic run with alll 4 characters yet, which the game all but tells you is hiding some Slay the Spire-esque final floor, or something of that sort. i'll reserve most of my judgment until then, but i still think this point stands, because as it is, there aren't really bosses so much as just a set amount of fights per floor, and having to beat 4 runs minimum to (maybe) have something like that would still be a bit unfortunate, imo. overall, tho, i'm genuinely enamored with the game so far and look forward to doing more runs! the game is quite satisfying to play, and i really do enjoy finding the best word to take advantage of the magicks i have in front of me on any given turn. definitely recommend for any word-game/roguelike enjoyers, especially any who are looking for gameplay that departs from the realm of Scrabble-esque point-maxing

So, basically, this is a word game. Okay, why not. I like this kind of games. BUT You can't type words that are 12+ letters long. You "fight" enemies with random powerups, 50% of them will actually hurt or kill you in your OWN "deck". Each enemy has a gimmick, for instance, there is one that will one shot you the next turn, if you don't kill yourself first with the negative effects on your letters. Another one limits your capacity to write maximum 6 letter words. So you can not inflict enough damage or heal enough, I dragged a fight for 40 minutes, using a power up that heals both player and the enemy for the same amount (what's the point apart dragging on, really....) before giving up on this one, it was absolutely impossible with only 6 letter words. An awful lot of words aren't recognized so I have to type whatever comes to mind until it just works. I don't want to be mean. There is a good idea behind this game, but there is no balance whatsoever. If what I said can frustrate you, well, you will be frustrated. If you don't mind it, play the game. EDIT : to add insult to injury, I managed to get to the 3rd world, just to discover that healing doesn't work, against an invincible enemy with too much armor and attack.

Enemies are too spongy, most of the "power-ups" actually hurt you instead of the enemy, the amount of damage you can do with your powerups is miniscule compared to the amount the enemy can do, and the rate at which you gain more powerups is painfully slow 5 is not enough. Basically completely unbalanced with the only redeeming factor being the art, and that's just personal preference. Needs to be worked on some more and rebalanced and it could be cool.

There are too many issues with this game as if they haven't even played it. Some of the enemies will just soft lock you from beating them or even hurting them. There are magics that don't work correctly and instead of doing what they say do the opposite. There are too many effects that reduce the fun of the game, and make it very frustrating to play. Getting your abilities stuck on letters like Z or Q or X and then not able to really use them in any ways outside of using one of your very limited rerolls. It's just really annoying and sucks the fun out of the game. The price is really good but it feels like a demo and not a full release.

Nothing but respect for the developer for trying something new and fresh. It is truly an amazing concept for a game, and I will keep an eye on their future games, but unfortunately the execution on this is not what I expected. If you want TL:DR, the game is just not fun, that's the core problem. It also feels like a quick game jam proof of concept, rather than a finished game. I would keep this game if it was an early access or a demo, but I'm kinda surprised this took two years. It is so bare bones, with stock animations and sound design (which I had to turn off), very few items, few attack types, very few art and enemies, who have no patterns, no types, just random everything. UI is also either very confusing, or very misleading, I would know which for sure if I figured out what it was trying to say in some cases. What the game promises is that your keys will have "quirks", some good, some bad, and you have to navigate your way and find a fitting word. In reality, you have mostly bad quirks, that are getting worse and worse, and sometimes game decides to spit out -1 damage for you to use (not always, believe it or not) on enemy with 20 health, while it does 6 in return, which somehow damages you with 9? and also burns 5 of your letters and then your vowels are gone? Even if you mitigate this and win, the game just straight up punishes you with "rewards". Each reward comes with a downside that is just agonizing, they can just kill your chances of finishing the run. They're just really really ♥♥♥♥♥♥, man. The "reward" system sucks so much. You just have no incentive to win the battle, there is nothing really good waiting for you, nothing you will get excited by. It's just not fun at all. This is the weirdest execution of the roguelike formula I've seen. If you want an example of what a battle in this game looks like: I faced an enemy who took away one of my letters each turn, and on each of my turns I would just get a single, one (1) attacking boon that did -1 damage, each time on "J" key. I just used the word "Just" 4 times and won the battle.

It's fun game, but it does suffer from being too random and unpredictable - there's not enough control to allow you to have more control.

If you're the sort of person who's enjoyed Wordle in the past then this a great roguelike for you that won't break the bank. A great aesthetic, joined by some great ideas and fun characters ties together this typing adventure that causes you to expand you vocabulary but not simply into big words, but ones that feel specific gaps. I have a written a much larger review here: https://backloggd.com/u/Psientologist/review/4524924/ Put simply, it's a recommendation from me even if the game is not quite in its perfect form.
Pretty good game overall. Thinking of words with the best combinations of letters is a good challenge.

I like this game quite a bit, although I agree with the points in some of the negative reviews. Positives: the art is charming and characterful, and *all* the mechanics serve to make the core gameplay interesting. You're trying to maximize some letters while avoiding others, and letter order often matters. This is the game, and it's fun! Negatives: Balance and variety are lacking. One magic is OP and can win runs by itself; a few enemies have a counter for it, but most don't. Other magics seem situational and underpowered. One character has special mechanics that don't allow the OP strat; he feels like a fun challenge mode. I think only one win with him is required for progression. After that, progression is just based on wins (with challenge modifiers, some of which do require changing tactics). Enemy variety is limited; different enemies share mechanics and can give you the same debuffs. It seems enemies can also appear anywhere in the three acts, which contributes to a lack of distinct identity for acts and enemies. But again, this criticism comes from a place of liking the game. I don't demand StS polish from a solo dev project asking $5 on sale. The dictionary could be improved; some short junk gets through, and some real words do not. Let me have susurrus!

Tomb of the Bloodletter is pretty fun ... until I encounter the enemy that locks away half my keyboard. I really want to like this game, however there are some design choices, or even oversights (?), that make my overall enjoyment suffer. Some of the combats are just plain unfun right now. These are things I believe can be ironed out, because the fundamentals are there and they are quite solid. I think my issues with the enemy I mentioned would be solved if the Magicks could only appear on the active half of your keyboard, for example. Being nerfed to less than half your power on turn 2 is VERY rough, especially if you encounter the boss version with 20 HP when you may only have one type of attack that does *1* damage. Not to mention that I think this enemy was not at all considered when making the Prophet. The lord should, in my opinion, not be able to demand you create a word that contains letters from both sides of the keyboard, when only one side is active.

This game is REALLY fun. It takes a simple word game and turns it into a maddening (positive) puzzle - I have happily stared at a given turn for like 10 minutes just to figure out how to optimize whatever word I'm picking. The different upsides and downsides you can apply to your letters are consistently meaningful (that is, the game feels well balanced), the art is silly and cute, and the structure of the run even requires your skill to optimize your path, which I think is really clever. The UI feels nice and the tutorial is helpful. I accidentally stayed up super late playing this and can't wait to dig in further! It scratches some kind of itch I didn't know I had right between NYT Spelling Bee and Balatro.

For someone like me who isn't good at spelling, this game is hard LOL. It is a word Balatro with similar styles to Slay the Spire 2. If you enjoy a hard rouge like thats also scrabble this is for you. Even though I think you have to be a masochist to play this for long stretches.... this game is incredibly fun and well designed. This game will make you think (or maybe im just kinda dumb LOL) Still this will keep me entertained for a while to come, I can play this and experience something different each time.
[FESS 7/12/25] Keep a dictionary handy as words are your weapons, tools, and create the paths for your adventure. Additionally, certain letters have different effects, so keep that in mind.
